card werk-mc-fork-nosession  [open]
A fork of a tab with no session opens an empty tab
why: A fork copies the session of the tab it comes from, and a tab that has never sent a message has none. Opening the tab anyway keeps the fork gesture working on every tab. The new tab then behaves like an empty conversation on the clicked card.

A fork copies the session of the tab it comes from. A tab that has sent no message has no session of its own. To keep the fork gesture from failing on such a tab, the fork opens the new tab anyway, on the clicked card, with no parent session. Its first message starts a new session with no history. The new tab keeps its home card (see #werk-mc-split).

This holds also for a tab that is itself a fork and has sent no message: it has no session of its own yet, so a fork of it starts empty too.

Example:

- tab A, homed on "#map", has sent no message.
- tab C, homed on "#map", has sent a message, so it has session s1.

1. The person forks A at "#fold". Tab B opens with home "#fold" and no parent session.
2. B sends its first message. Its agent starts a new session, with no history.
3. The person forks C at "#fold". Nothing changes from the normal fork: tab D opens with parent s1, and its first message continues from a copy of s1.

    A "#map" (no session) --fork--> B "#fold" (parent: none) --first message--> new, empty session
    C "#map" (session s1) --fork--> D "#fold" (parent: s1)   --first message--> copy of s1

card werk-mc-empty-control  [open]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
A separate control in the tab strip starts an empty conversation in a new tab
why: A fork brings the parent's history, which is wrong for an unrelated topic. One press must give a clean conversation. It always opens a new tab, because a switch to an existing tab would show an old conversation instead.

A fork carries the parent's whole history (see #werk-mc-fork). That is wrong for an unrelated topic. To give that topic a clean start, the tab strip has a second control next to '+' (see #werk-mc-open for '+'). The empty control opens a new tab at the open card, with no parent session. The first message in that tab starts a session with no history. No other gesture starts a conversation empty.

The empty control never switches to an existing tab. A fork switches to a tab that already has the card as its home. The empty control opens a new tab every time, also on that card. The new tab still takes the open card as its home and its chip label (see #werk-mc-split).

Example:

- tab "main", home card "#map", active. The map shows "#fold".
- tab "fold", home card "#fold".

1. The person Shift+clicks a link to "#fold". The pane switches to tab "fold". No tab opens.
2. The person goes back to "main". The map shows "#fold" again.
3. The person presses the empty control. A second "#fold" chip opens and becomes active. Its conversation has no history.

Two ways to fix them:

1. **Make the renderer draw indented code blocks too** (recommended). This is one code change. It fixes all 13 cards now, and the next pipeline run cannot break pictures this way.
2. **Stage a proposal on each of the 13 cards** to put its picture in a fence. That is 13 accepts for you, and the cause stays.

lp-rubric: proposed

A rubric is the loop's stop condition. There are two, and the loop picks by what happens to the output: #lp-rubric-proto when the artifact is thrown away after it answers a question, #lp-rubric-prod when the code is merged.

**Both are built into werk.** Not files in the repo being judged, not drafted per project, not derived per work item. Two constants the tool ships with.

Each has three sections, and the split is what makes a rubric usable:

==```==
checks        deterministic — a command, an exit code, no model (#lp-two)judgements    an agent grades each, because no exit code answers themheld-out      withheld from the builder, run once at the end (#lp-split)
==```==

The production rubric has all three. The prototype rubric has no held-out section — held-out exists to stop a builder gaming a bar it can see, and a throwaway accumulates nothing worth gaming.

**Written once, not per work item.** That is the property the rejected options give up. A rubric re-derived per run needs approval per run, and the recurring human input is exactly what the rubric exists to remove.

**The cost of hardcoding, stated so it is not a surprise.** #lp-rubric-prod's checks name `bun`, `tsc` and playwright; its judgements name `.werk/log.jsonl` and the werk CLI. Pointing the loop at a second project means editing werk's source. That is the moment #lp-rubric:opt3 stops being deferred.

Deferred: #lp-rubric:opt3 (a prototype.md and production.md file in each project, drafted from the repo and corrected once). Not rejected — it is what the hardcoded pair becomes once a second project exists.

Rejected: #lp-rubric:opt0 (derived per work item, approved at a gate). #lp-rubric:opt1 (project baseline plus per-item additions — the per-item part is where a builder would negotiate its own bar).
lp-rubric-proto: proposed

The bar for an artifact that gets thrown away after it answers a question.

## checks

==```==
the artifact exists at the declared pathits entry point exits 0, if it has one
==```==

## judgements

==```==
the artifact answers the question the fork asked, and nothing morewhere the brief was silent, the reading it chose is stated in one linenothing was written outside the worktree or scratch dir (#al-ephem)
==```==

Judgement 2 is the no-questions contract already in src/prototype.ts made checkable: a headless build cannot stop at a question, so it picks and says so. A prototype that silently picked is worth less than one that picked and named the pick.

## not checked, on purpose

==```==
coverage, lint, doc comments, naming, dead code, commit hygiene
==```==

This section is what makes a prototype rubric worth writing at all. Without it a builder carries production habits into a throwaway, and the prototype stops being cheap — which removes the only reason to build one instead of arguing about it.

There is no held-out section. Held-out exists to stop a builder gaming a bar it can see (#lp-split). Nothing is merged here and nothing accumulates, so there is no bar worth gaming.

test           the unit teststest:coverage  the same tests, with the project's own threshold enforcedtypecheck      the strongest static pass the language offerslint           the style and static-analysis passe2e            the product driven end to end, against a real build

I cannot reproduce this from the code alone. In the prototype, a fork of a parked tab whose process was stopped already works the way you expect. The new tab records the parent's session, and its first message resumes and forks it. The refusal comes only when the source tab has no session id in memory. Two paths lead there:

1. The tab has never sent a message, and it is not a fork itself.
2. You pressed "Clear context" in that tab. This clears the session on purpose.

The rule you describe is the rule in `#werk-mc-fork`, so no card has to change. This is a bug in the prototype, or a third path that I have not found.

Which tab did you fork from? Did that tab show messages, and did you clear its context before you forked?
